feedback: If a learner maps the loop onto a simple on/off thermostat and concludes the body is a switch: switch to the cruise-control version and ask how a car eases up and down a hill without fully stopping and starting.
If a learner cannot locate the effector: ask which part actually DOES the correcting action, separating 'deciding' (control centre) from 'acting' (effector).
activities.intendedInsight: The generic negative-feedback structure (sensor → control centre → effector → response toward setpoint) is the same across familiar machines and body systems; a continuously-adjusting controller models biological regulation better than an on/off switch.
learnerActions: Study a non-biological controller such as a car's cruise-control (or a thermostat) and identify what senses the speed, what decides, and what acts to restore it.
Match each part of the controller onto the biological loop: sensor/receptor, control centre, effector, setpoint, response.

Explain why cruise-control, which eases the throttle up and down continuously in response to going too fast or too slow, is a better analogy than a simple on/off thermostat for showing that the body corrects smoothly rather than snapping fully on and off.
activities.title: Map a familiar controller onto the biological loop

feedback: If a learner treats the two systems as doing the same job the same way: ask them to time a reflex versus a growth response and name which signal type fits each.
If a learner assumes the nervous system is always involved: point to glucose regulation, which is hormonal, as a response that does not need a nerve signal.
If a learner mixes up the attributes: have them re-sort speed/signal/duration into the correct column before placing examples.
activities.intendedInsight: The nervous and endocrine systems are complementary, not identical: nerve signals are fast, electrical and short-lived while hormones are slower, chemical and longer-lasting, and each suits different kinds of task. Not every homeostatic response involves nerves — some are purely endocrine.
learnerActions: Compare the two communication channels on three dimensions: speed (fast vs slow), nature of signal (electrical vs chemical) and duration (short-lived vs long-lasting).
Decide which channel fits pulling your hand off a hot pan, and explain why a fast electrical nerve signal is right for that.
Decide which channel fits controlling growth over years or the hours-long glucose response after a meal, and explain why a slower chemical hormone suits that.
Build a two-column comparison and place each example in the column that fits, justifying each placement.
activities.title: Contrast nervous and endocrine signalling with fitting scenarios

feedback: If a learner picks 'always makes a value smaller': return them to the low-glucose/glucagon case and ask what direction the correction went there.
If a learner mis-orders the loop: ask what must be detected before anything can act, separating sensing from responding.
If a learner labels a hormonal response as nervous: have them check whether the signal is electrical and fast or chemical and slower.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, independently-stated understanding that negative feedback opposes change in either direction toward a setpoint, that glucose regulation is hormonal, and that nervous and endocrine signalling differ by speed, mechanism and duration.
learnerActions: Put the loop stages in the correct order: stimulus → sensor → control centre → effector → response returning the variable toward setpoint.
Sort a set of responses into 'nervous' or 'endocrine', justifying each choice by speed and signal type.
Answer a question whose tempting wrong option says 'negative feedback always makes a value smaller', and explain why the correct answer is that it opposes deviation in EITHER direction.
For a given high glucose level, choose how much insulin should be released and explain the reasoning linking the amount of correction to the size of the deviation.
activities.title: Check and consolidate the loop and the contrast

feedback: If a learner recites steps without the principle: ask 'why is this called negative even though it keeps you healthy?' to prompt the opposing-the-change idea.
If a learner cannot transfer to temperature: ask them to name the sensor, the effector (e.g. sweating to cool, shivering to warm) and the direction of correction, checking it against the same loop.
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed to justify each step helps surface whether the learner holds the self-correcting principle or is reciting the loop by rote, and supports transfer of the pattern from glucose to temperature.
learnerActions: Take the role of explaining to someone (or 'talking to your own pancreas') what happens, step by step, after a sugary meal.
Answer a probing follow-up: if a response made glucose rise even HIGHER instead of lowering it, what kind of feedback would that be (positive feedback) and why would it be dangerous?
Explain whether getting too hot and cooling down fits the same detect-and-oppose pattern as glucose control.
activities.title: Reason aloud about the loop in a questioning dialogue
